extracted.intended_audience: industrialists, business managers, philanthropic organizers, trade school and hospital administrators, and railroad managers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidelines for organizing industry, philanthropic institutions (trade schools and hospitals), and railroads so they are service-oriented, self-sustaining, efficient, and promote individual self-reliance. Emphasizes practical, factory-style management, financial prudence, and humane institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropy should promote self-reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity that does not aim to make itself unnecessary is not performing service; philanthropy which merely gives and thus encourages idleness creates dependence and resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'doing things for people' that coddle them into helplessness; favor efforts that make recipients self-supporting. Beware that much 'charity' is not genuine and often belittles both giver and receiver. Redirect charitable funds toward productive enterprises that enable people to earn a living rather than become permanent objects of bounty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry organized for service and subdivision of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry should be organized to provide productive places for all, including the maimed, halt, and blind; minute subdivision of industry permits many roles so that nearly anyone can earn an adequate living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design production so tasks match workers' abilities—avoid wasteful assignments (e.g., putting able-bodied men in jobs fillable by cripples, or blind people at basket-weaving when better options exist). Replace useless, punitive labour (e.g., convicts breaking stone) with productive work. The aim is maximum service at minimum cost and to make philanthropy unnecessary by integrating the non-productive into productive roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade school pedagogical principles (three cardinal principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade school should (1) keep the boy a boy and not make him a premature working-man, (2) combine academic training with industrial instruction, and (3) give the boy pride and responsibility by training him on articles of recognized industrial worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid makeshift manual-training that offers only a smattering of knowledge. Ensure schooling trains boys to be productive—work on real parts used by industry rather than throwaway exercises. Preserve boyhood (appropriate social/age handling) while preparing them for skilled work. Use marks in industry to adjust scholarships and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade school as experiential learning using the industrial plant
rubrics_metrics.description: The industrial plant should be the text-book: concrete shop problems teach arithmetic; engine rooms and shipments illustrate geography and world commerce; physics and chemistry become laboratory practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure instruction so class lessons and shop work reinforce each other. Arrange continuous classes with shop rotations (e.g., blocks of one week class, two weeks shop). Progress pupils machine-by-machine, teaching observation and purpose; have them repair and care for machinery, do pattern-making, and perform inspected work that the company purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade school financial structure and student accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Operate trade school on scholarships and thrift: award annual cash scholarships (in example, $400 increasing to $600), require monthly savings deposits into a thrift fund, and record class/shop/industry marks used to adjust scholarship amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the school self-sustaining where possible; inspected (accepted) work may be purchased by the company and losses borne by the school. Use savings accounts to teach thrift; require savings to remain unless emergency permission granted. Organize school finances so it can pay its way and avoid dependence on charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitals should be self-supporting and serve moderate-paying patients without stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: Design hospitals to be self-supporting, offering maximum service at minimum cost and without the colouring of charity; provide private, identical rooms grouped uniformly so every patient is on equal footing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the extremes of hospitals only for the rich or only for the poor; provide a middle option for those who can pay modestly but resent charity. Eliminate wards, standardize rooms and furnishings, and remove choice that introduces inequality. Plan for expansion only as facilities justify themselves and aim to cover depreciation though not necessarily return profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed hospital model with salaried staff and patient-first orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ all physicians and nurses by the year; staff must have no outside practice or financial interest in patients so that patient interest is primary. The hospital assumes full responsibility for in-patient care, while cooperating with family physicians when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay salaries equal to or greater than private practice to remove perverse incentives. Avoid the notion that a patient is property of a doctor; prohibit outside doctors from practicing while the patient is inpatient. This reduces financial conflicts and the tendency to prolong treatment for revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission and diagnostic procedures: multiple independent examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon admission a patient is examined by the senior physician and then routed through several physicians who each make complete, independent examinations and submit written findings to the head physician without consulting each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independently obtained multiple diagnoses (three to seven) to ensure, within present knowledge limits, a correct diagnosis. Keep a complete record of the case and take steps so wrong diagnoses are more readily detected and corrected than under customary 'professional etiquette' that protects initial diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital operations: factory-style efficiency and fixed cost-accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage hospitals like factories: group patients by nursing needs, design floors to minimize waste motion, set fixed charges (room, board, medical, nursing) with no extras, and maintain a cost system to regulate charges to make ends meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit nurse loads (no more than seven patients per nurse; typical grouping might be one nurse to two or to five patients depending on need). Save steps and time by floor layout. Fixed pricing examples provided ($4.50/day room+board+medical+nursing; $125 major operation) but charges are tentative and will be adjusted by cost accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage self-reliance; eliminate coddling and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Coddling is a drug; removing fear (dependence on outside circumstances or favors) fosters self-reliance. The habit of failure is mental—success requires 'stick-to-it-iveness' rather than wisdom or money alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage people to avoid dependence on employers' moods; either become one's own boss or learn to overcome fears and win freedom where one previously surrendered it. Promote vision, persistence, and internal responsibility rather than providing external safety nets that create dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroads should be managed by capable railroad men, not bankers or lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroads have been turned from service enterprises into vehicles of finance and legal manipulation; bankers and lawyers, who often know little of the business, displaced active managers and hampered effective operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restore practical management authority to those who know railroading. Reduce rule-bound, counsel-driven operation that substitutes legalistic safety for common-sense decisions; allow managers to run operations according to circumstances and practical knowledge rather than only legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate borrowing and speculative finance; reinvest earnings in rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive borrowing and speculative flotation of securities has led to receiverships and misdirected priorities; more earnings should be used to rehabilitate properties rather than finance inside speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not borrow to cover management errors. Reinvest net revenue into maintenance and rehabilitation (track, rolling stock, shops) rather than using earnings to support speculative insiders. Historical examples: capitalization per mile drastically reduced in reorganizations; avoid pyramiding securities that make the structure topheavy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize legal and administrative bloat; simplify organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive legal departments, over-large executive/administrative offices, and needless titles create waste; settle outstanding claims reasonably and cut unnecessary accounting and red tape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidate administrative functions (e.g., close extraneous executive offices), reduce legal expense (example: from nearly $18,000/month to about $200/month by prompt factual settlement), and abolish offices/titles not required by law. Streamline organization to reduce payroll and wasted overhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empower personal responsibility; break the 'awaiting orders' culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Railway staff often wait for hierarchical orders rather than acting; cultivate a culture where individuals take initiative and are expected to perform throughout an eight-hour day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay for an eight-hour day and expect eight hours' work; if tasks finish early, assign other duties for the remainder of the shift. Allow managers/frontline workers to make on-the-spot decisions (e.g., clear wrecks without waiting for orders). Use flexibility for compensatory time (deduct overtime from future days or allow a whole day off) rather than automatic overtime pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational efficiency: rehabilitate track and rolling stock and improve supply quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reballast track, lay new rails, overhaul locomotives/rolling stock in-house, and buy better-quality supplies to reduce waste and improve reliability and transit times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out rehabilitation from earnings rather than large external infusions. Improve procurement quality: saving on supplies by buying better qualities and eliminating waste. Measure performance with concrete metrics (example: reduced freight transit from 8-9 days to 3.5 days to major eastern cities). Treat idle cars on sidings as operational questions to be solved, not ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor efficiency and staffing: reduce payroll and raise per-worker productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut unnecessary employees in offices, shops, and on roads; set a minimum wage (example: $6/day), eliminate extra men, and increase individual productivity so fewer men do the work previously done by many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industrial efficiency to accomplish more with fewer personnel (example: one shop where 20 men now do more work than 59 did before). Organize track gangs and crews to be lean and productive (example: 16-man gang outperforming 40-man gang). Avoid padding payroll with nonessential positions.
